ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.title: Unpaid Land Compensation on the Coastal Embankment Polders
ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.place: Polders 32 and 33, Dacope upazila, Khulna district, and polders 35/1 and 35/3, Bagerhat district, Bangladesh
ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.point: Dacope, the upazila holding polders 32 and 33 of the first works package (OpenStreetMap place point for Dacope, Khulna district)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-52800 for the First Phase of the Coastal Embankment Improvement Project (P128276). US$375 million approved 26 June 2013. The credit disbursed US$311.84 million. Original closing was 31 December 2020; actual closing was 31 December 2023. The original total project cost of US$400 million was cut to US$375.74 million after US$24.26 million of the credit, or SDR 18.223 million, was cancelled 17 days before closing. The scope was cut from 17 polders to 10 in January 2020. Environmental category A. The implementing agency was the Bangladesh Water Development Board. The project financed land acquisition and the resettlement and rehabilitation of people adversely affected by it (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2024; IEG ICR Review ICRR0024220, 30 November 2024).

lenders.name: Pilot Program for Climate Resilience, Strategic Climate Fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-14713 of US$25 million alongside the IDA credit; US$24,999,892.29 disbursed. Total disbursement across the credit and the grant was US$336.84 million as of 15 May 2024 (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2024).

ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.community: The project raised and widened embankments around coastal polders, which required private land and moved people living on the existing embankments. At appraisal the census survey of February 2012 found the first works package alone would affect 6,203 households and persons in their homes, places of business and other assets, plus 184 common resource structures, most of them on the existing embankments. The completion report states that by project close the project had made significant progress on land acquisition and compensation payments and that no construction was carried out until the process was complete. It then records that as of April 2024, four months after the credit closed, land acquisition payment stood at 92.4 per cent. The ICR Review adds that the Bank task team put the figure at 94 per cent as of June 2024 and that there was no further update after that. The unpaid balance was attributed to incomplete embankment works, compensation amounts as small as BDT 345, about US$4.00, and missing proof of ownership, including unavailable mauza maps, khatians, transfer and succession documents and possession records, as well as disputed claims and parcels under court cases. Responsibility for finishing the payments was left after closing to the project's key focal point, the executive engineers of the Bangladesh Water Development Board's operation and maintenance divisions and the Deputy Commissioner offices of the districts concerned. The Bank task team told the Independent Evaluation Group that the interim government changed the district administrations, including the Deputy Commissioners responsible for land acquisition payment, several times. Under the first works package 291 female-headed households were affected by resettlement and under the second works package 478; the completion report says the women heading those households received relocation and resettlement benefits and a grant. Thirty-six grievance redress committees were set up across the first two packages and received 269 complaints by 31 December 2023, all of which were closed. The completion report also states that resettlement assistance for involuntarily displaced people without title was completed before works started on each section. Financial management shortcomings forfeited US$12.69 million of concessional IDA funding, made up of US$6.24 million from an undocumented designated account and US$6.45 million left undisbursed.
ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,325 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The nearest figure in the Bank's own documents is the appraisal count of 6,203 households and persons affected in the first works package, from the February 2012 census survey in the Project Appraisal Document. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2023 with land acquisition payment incomplete. The Bank task team reported 94 per cent paid as of June 2024 and acknowledged no further update since that date. The completion report of 28 June 2024 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 November 2024 reached the same rating on a split evaluation.

ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.confidence_note: The lending terms, the payment percentages and their dates, and the appraisal affected-household count all come from the Bank's own completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it and the appraisal document. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of these payments was found. The 94 per cent is not in a document at all: the review attributes it to the Bank task team. No document found names the households still unpaid, says how many they are, or gives a count of people actually relocated. The 92.4 and 94 per cent figures are percentages of payment value or of parcels, which the documents do not define. The completion report also states that no construction was carried out until the land acquisition process was complete.

lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.title: Shop Removals on the Shahi Guzargah, Walled City of Lahore
lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.place: Shahi Guzargah (Royal Trail), from Delhi Gate past the Wazir Khan Mosque and Shahi Hammam, Walled City of Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.point: Wazir Khan Mosque on the Shahi Guzargah, the historic street the works ran along (OpenStreetMap point for the mosque)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-73800 for the Punjab Municipal Services Improvement Project (P083929). US$50 million approved 1 June 2006, loan agreement signed 5 June 2006. The completion report's financing table gives US$48.85 million disbursed, 97.70 per cent of appraisal, with the borrower contributing US$5.74 million against US$8.90 million at appraisal; its data sheet gives the disbursed amount as US$48.86 million. Closing was extended twice, by 23 months in the restructuring of 2 August 2010 and by a further 12 months to 30 November 2013. Component 2 financed the pilot works in the Walled City of Lahore, including the Resettlement Action Plan. The completion report of 19 May 2014 rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Substantial. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 2 June 2015 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, overall Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Significant and the quality of the completion report Unsatisfactory.

lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.community: The project paid for the first stage of rebuilding the Shahi Guzargah, a 1.6 km historic street through the Walled City of Lahore, together with the facades, street surfacing, water supply, sewerage, drainage and electrical network along it. Surveys for the Resettlement Action Plan found 147 shops, counting sub-units, that had to be removed completely, 732 more shops that would be affected temporarily along the Shahi Guzargah, and 264 encroachments onto public space, mainly kitchens and washrooms, in the 47 residential streets running off it. The plan records who held the 147 shops: 84 belonged to the Auqaf Department, 22 to the Municipal Corporation, 18 to informal occupants and 10 were privately owned; 28 of the shopkeepers were owners, 76 non-resident owners, 8 resident tenants, 11 non-resident tenants and 22 were in an 'others' category. It also counted 79 day-seller shops, 10 khokhas (kiosks), 2 tharas and 19 mixed cases among the temporary sellers who would have to be compensated, and 53 employees working in the shops, whose families the plan put at 371 people. The plan states that no person was to be affected through an impact on houses or residences; the impacts it counts are on business premises and livelihoods. Of the 147 shopkeepers, 50 were earning between Rs 5,000 and Rs 20,000 a month and 61 between Rs 21,000 and Rs 35,000. Payments were to be made by cross cheque through the Revenue Department, to people with documentary proof of ownership. Employees of permanently displaced shops were to get a one-off Rs 15,000 and employees of temporarily disturbed shops Rs 6,000. By closing, the completion report records that 147 shops and 264 encroachments had been removed and 732 shops had been given temporary support, after more than a thousand meetings with shopkeepers, traders and residents. At closing the facade work was 72 per cent complete and street surfacing 52 per cent, with the rest finished using Government of Punjab funds.
lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,153 for this project. That figure is the plan-stage estimate in the Resettlement Action Plan itself, which states: 'Based on 879 shops/owners of the property being affected from minor to severe degrees with average family size of 7 persons, there would be impact on 6153 persons due to the project implementation in the Pilot Project area.' It is an estimate of people affected, arrived at by multiplying affected shops by an assumed household size, and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 147 shops removed completely, 264 encroachments removed and 732 shops given temporary support. No Bank document found counts people or households relocated: the Resettlement Action Plan states that no person was to be affected through an impact on houses or residences.
lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.outcome: The loan closed on 30 November 2013 with the street works unfinished and completed afterwards with provincial funds. The Independent Evaluation Group rated the resettlement work a successful pilot. No independent follow-up study of what happened to the 147 shopkeepers after removal was found.

lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.confidence_note: The counts of shops removed, encroachments removed and shops temporarily supported come from the Bank's own completion report, and the ownership, income and entitlement detail from the project's Resettlement Action Plan, which the borrower prepared. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of the removals was found. The aftermath is not on the record: no document found records how much was actually paid to the 147 shopkeepers or the 53 employees, whether any were relocated to new premises, or what their incomes were afterwards. A master plan for 173 replacement shops is mentioned in the plan but no document found says it was built. The plan's own breakdowns of the 147 do not sum to 147: the ownership-status categories come to 145 and the income bands to 141, and the plan does not reconcile them.

nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.title: Compensation Left Unpaid on the Nepal Road Sector Development Project
nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.place: Beneficiary districts of the Road Sector Development Project, including Kalikot, Bajhang and Jumla, Nepal
nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.point: Jumla, one of the three original target districts the completion report names, and the sixth poorest district in Nepal on its own account (OpenStreetMap administrative point for Jumla)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits and grants IDA-48320, IDA-50020, IDA-58650, IDA-H3390 and IDA-H6290 for the Road Sector Development Project (P095977). Grant IDA-H3390 of US$42.6 million approved 6 December 2007 and effective 21 February 2008, with the five instruments together originally committing US$172.6 million, revised to US$128,515,589.07 and US$126,444,071 disbursed. The completion report puts the total project cost at US$174,004,274, including US$47,560,204 from the borrower; the Independent Evaluation Group's data sheet instead labels US$126,444,070, the Bank disbursement, as the total project cost. Original closing was 30 June 2012; actual closing was 15 January 2020. Category B. The implementing agency was the Department of Roads. The project carried out a programme of compensation, resettlement and rehabilitation of displaced persons. Compliance with both social and environmental safeguards policies was rated Moderately Satisfactory at the last implementation support mission in November and December 2019; monitoring and evaluation quality was rated Modest (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 September 2020; IEG ICR Review ICRR0022396, 22 February 2021).

companies.name: Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats Pvt. Ltd.
companies.role: Indian consulting firm that prepared the detailed survey and design and the Resettlement Action Plan for the Satbanjh-Jhulaghat road under the project's Phase I, in association with Nepali firms (Resettlement Action Plan, September 2007).

companies.name: Full Bright Consultancy (Pvt.) Ltd.
companies.role: Nepali consultancy, in joint venture with Soil Test (P) Ltd and Himal Integrated Consultancy (P) Ltd, associated in preparing the Satbanjh-Jhulaghat road survey, design and Resettlement Action Plan (Resettlement Action Plan, September 2007).

nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.community: The project upgraded dry-season roads and tracks to all-season standard and maintained highway and feeder roads, scaled up from about 297 km to 700 km of upgrading. Its social impacts were land acquisition leading to involuntary resettlement, loss of strips of land, loss of structures, disturbance and disruption of livelihoods, and loss of common property resources. Cash compensation was paid in full for 91 project-affected households, for 76 land parcels and 48 structures. For the remaining 24 households, holding 19 land parcels and 11 structures - 115 households across the report's two figures - compensation was still outstanding at closing because the households had not supplied the documents and clearance needed for payment. The money for 22 of those 24 households had been deposited at their district administration offices; for the other two, payment awaited a determination by the Compensation Determining Committee, after which the Department of Roads was to place the amount in an escrow account. Financial management was downgraded to moderately unsatisfactory in 2018-19, partly over non-compliance with contract terms on a 5 per cent mobilisation advance. One road under the project, Satbanjh-Jhulaghat, had its own Resettlement Action Plan in September 2007, which counted 73 affected households on that road alone, of which 7 were severely affected and about 5 were Dalit households among the vulnerable groups.
nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5,824 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 91 project-affected households paid in full and 24 still owed, 115 across its two figures, and the one road-level resettlement plan opened here counts 73 affected households on the Satbanjh-Jhulaghat road. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.outcome: The credit closed on 15 January 2020 with compensation unpaid to 24 households. The completion report leaves the final payments to the district administration offices and the Compensation Determining Committee, and no later document found records whether they were made.

The lender is therefore the only source for the harm and no independent account was found. swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.title: Land and Structures Taken for the Swat Right-Bank Road
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.place: Provincial highway S3-B, the Chakdara to Kanju section on the right bank of the Swat river, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.point: Chakdara, the southern end of the 40.9 km of highway S3-B reconstructed under the project (OpenStreetMap town point)

lenders.name: World Bank, as administrator of the Multi Donor Trust Fund for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, FATA and Balochistan
lenders.role: Grants TF-10112, TF-15895 and TF-16992 for the MDTF KP Emergency Roads Recovery Project (P125584). Original commitment US$8.0 million, approved 23 August 2011 and effective 17 October 2011; first additional financing of US$9.1 million approved 15 January 2014 and second of US$9.0 million approved 30 May 2014; revised amount US$26.10 million and US$25.62 million disbursed. Closing ran from 30 June 2014 for the first phase to 31 October 2015 for the third. Category B. Trust fund money is not normally usable for compensation, so approval was sought and given to pay compensation for lost assets and lost production from the grant funds. The completion report of 11 August 2016 rated outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Satisfactory, and risk to development outcome Significant; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 February 2017 agreed on outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance and gave risk to development outcome as Substantial. The two documents also give different approval and closing dates: the completion report's data sheet gives approval of the first phase as 23 August 2011 and the last closing as 31 October 2015, while the Independent Evaluation Group's data sheet gives Bank approval as 16 July 2011 and actual closing as 12 December 2015. The completion report's own data sheet names the first grant TF-10112 in its header and TF-10122 in its key dates table; TF-10112 is the number the Independent Evaluation Group uses.

swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.community: The project reconstructed 40.9 km of provincial highway S3-B from Chakdara to Kanju on the right bank of the Swat river, plus link roads, after a military operation and floods. The road serves a population of about 300,000 people on the right bank. The section of the same highway from Kanju to Madyan was funded by USAID and is not part of this project. The project paper for the first phase estimated that 498 people would be directly affected, about 3.75 acres of land would be acquired with crop-loss compensation on a further 1.75 acres where farmers had encroached on the right of way, 1,000 trees would be lost and 158 structures affected. The completion report gives the outcome: in Phase I, 114 people were affected, 1.6 acres of land in all were acquired or reclaimed, 74 trees were lost and 24 structures. In Phase II, 88 people were affected, crops were lost over 4.5 acres, and 731 trees and 23 structures were lost. In Phase III, 12 people were affected with very small losses. Those three phase figures come to 214 affected people; the report gives no total of its own. The completion report states that 98 per cent of affected parties had been compensated by the time it was written; the remainder were absent and had not responded to efforts to reach them. Its own summary says 'virtually all persons who lost property were compensated'. It also records 'delays in compensation payment at times', and says that when the provincial highway authority pulled its Deputy Director for Environment and Resettlement out of the project management unit for five months there were delays in handling grievance cases and in paying compensation. The report adds that the provincial government appears reluctant to devote staff and resources to social and environmental compliance. Grievance redress committees made up of affected people dealt with disputes over land ownership, compensation and payment delays. Auditors engaged by the provincial highway authority reviewed all three phases and reported a high degree of compliance.
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5,398 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts affected people phase by phase - 114, 88 and 12, 214 together - against 498 estimated for Phase I at the project-paper stage. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.outcome: The last grant closed on 31 October 2015 with 2 per cent of affected parties uncompensated because they could not be found. The project's savings on compensation and land acquisition, which came in below the amounts provided for, were used to build additional lengths of road.

sources.title: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Emergency Road Recovery Project (P125584)
Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, PK: KP Emergency Roads Recovery Project (P125584)

swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.confidence_note: The affected-person counts, acreages, tree and structure counts and the 98 per cent compensation figure come from the Bank's own completion report, which reports the implementing agency's figures; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report adds no resettlement detail. The lender is therefore reporting on its own project and no independent account of this road's land acquisition was found. The harm is small in scale. The report names no affected person, gives no compensation rate, does not say how long the payment delays ran, and does not convert the 2 per cent left uncompensated into a number of people. It also states that virtually all persons who lost property were compensated.

siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.title: Land and Structures Lost to the Siddhirganj Gas Pipeline and Transmission Line
siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.place: Siddhirganj power plant, Narayanganj, with the gas pipeline from Bakhrabad through Cumilla and Narayanganj districts and the transmission line through Konapara and Demra, Bangladesh
siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.point: The Electricity Generation Company of Bangladesh plant site at Siddhirganj, the project's generating site (OpenStreetMap industrial point named for the EGCB plant)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-45080 and IDA-57370 for the Siddhirganj Power Project, originally the Siddhirganj Peaking Power Project (P095965). IDA-45080: US$350 million, which the Bank's project record dates to Board approval on 30 October 2008; the financing agreement was signed on 13 November 2008 and the project became effective on 31 March 2009. The credit was revised to US$332,621,020 and US$309,875,467 disbursed. IDA-57370: US$176,710,000, revised to US$115,501,477 and US$112,652,157 disbursed. Total Bank financing US$526,710,000 original, US$422,527,624 disbursed. The borrower's planned contribution of US$312,890,000 is recorded as nil disbursed. Original closing 31 March 2016; actual closing 31 December 2019. Environmental category A, full assessment. The completion report rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory on a split rating and Bank performance Satisfactory. The completion report notes that the resettlement and rehabilitation costs under the gas transmission and power grid components were not financed by the World Bank (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: Gas Transmission Company Limited (GTCL)
companies.role: State-owned company that built the gas pipeline component and, through a contracted organisation, paid compensation to the people affected by it (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: Power Grid Company of Bangladesh (PGCB)
companies.role: State-owned company that built the transmission line component and changed the line route after objections; unable under government rules to acquire private land permanently, it paid only crop and temporary-loss compensation to private landowners (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: Electricity Generation Company of Bangladesh (EGCB)
companies.role: State-owned company that built the power station, signed the engineering, procurement and construction contracts with a joint-venture consortium the completion report does not name, and built the replacement school building (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: NTPC Limited
companies.role: Government of India enterprise that holds the operation and maintenance contract for the plant, concluded with EGCB (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

companies.name: Development Organization for the Rural Poor (DORP)
companies.role: Organisation engaged to carry out the resettlement of the people affected by the gas pipeline and to deliver GTCL's compensation to them (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 September 2020).

siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.community: The project built a power station at Siddhirganj, a gas pipeline to feed it and a transmission line to carry its output. The gas pipeline required permanent acquisition of 46.05 hectares of land and temporary requisition of 85.00 hectares along the alignment. In the paragraph on gas pipeline resettlement the completion report records 'a total of 1,501 entitled persons were affected by the Project'; 93 of them lost structures, one lost a poultry farm and one lost a pond, and 201 female-headed households were affected. People losing approximately 20 per cent of their assets were treated as vulnerable and put into a livelihood restoration programme of cash grants and skills training. Handover of the pipeline right of way was itself delayed: the Narayanganj and Cumilla district administrations began handing over land only in mid-May 2012. On the transmission line, people living on the planned right of way objected to the route because of its impact in dense residential areas. The line was moved. The old route would have affected 72 families on private and public land; the route chosen instead affected 19 families, most of them squatting on public land and on private agricultural or industrial land. Because government rules barred the power grid company from permanently acquiring private land, the private landowners on the line were not compensated for their land at all. They kept ownership and received only compensation for crops and related temporary losses during construction. Across the grid and pipeline works the completion report says over 20,000 project-affected households were compensated for permanent and temporary impacts to land, land use and crops or livelihoods. Noise and emissions from the plant were found to put a nearby school and its students at risk, and a new school building was built at a safe distance and handed to the Bangladesh Power Development Board.
siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4,444 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 1,501 entitled persons affected by the project, in its paragraph on gas pipeline resettlement, and 19 families affected by the transmission line route that was built, against 72 families on the route that was dropped. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.outcome: The credits closed on 31 December 2019. The transmission line was rerouted after objections, cutting the families affected from 72 to 19. Private landowners along the line retained title but were never paid for the land itself. Resettlement and rehabilitation costs on the pipeline and grid components were borne outside the Bank's financing.

siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.confidence_note: The hectares, the 1,501 entitled persons, the 93 who lost structures, the 201 female-headed households and the statement that private landowners were not compensated for their land all come from the Bank's own completion report. No Independent Evaluation Group review and no independent account of this resettlement were found, so the lender is the only source. What is thin is who those people are and where: the report gives no village names beyond Siddhirganj-Konapara in Demra for the transmission line, does not say what the 19 families on the chosen route lost, and does not break the 'over 20,000 households' figure down or say what each was paid. The joint-venture consortium that built the plant is not named in any document opened. The 30 October 2008 approval date is from the Bank's project record, not from either document.

gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.title: Two-Year Gap Between Acquisition and Compensation Notices on the Gujarat Highways
gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.place: Eight state highway widening and strengthening corridors in Gujarat, which the documents do not name individually, India
gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.point: Gandhinagar, seat of the Gujarat Roads and Buildings Department that ran the project; the documents opened do not name which of the eight widening corridors the land was acquired on (OpenStreetMap city point for Gandhinagar, Gujarat)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-83130 for the Second Gujarat State Highway Project (P114827). US$175 million approved 13 December 2013, loan agreement dated 12 February 2014, and the full loan amount disbursed. Original closing 31 January 2019, extended by 23 months in the restructuring of 13 September 2018; the project closed 31 December 2020. The borrower's contribution was US$158.50 million and the private sector's US$37.40 million. Component A, Highway Improvement, financed the road works and, within both of its sub-components, support for land acquisition and resettlement, utility relocation, environmental management and supervision. The appraisal document states that all land acquisition and resettlement costs paid in cash were to be met from Government of Gujarat funds, with Bank money covering the consultancies, goods and works for carrying out the resettlement plans. Classified Category A and triggered the Bank's policies on involuntary resettlement, indigenous peoples, forests and physical cultural resources (IEG ICR Review ICRR0022895, 13 June 2022; World Bank Project Appraisal Document, 7 November 2013).

gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.community: The project widened and strengthened eight road corridors and rehabilitated three more added at the September 2018 restructuring: 60.4 km from Radhanpur to Chanasma, 66.8 km from Mehsana to Palanpur including a 5 km bypass at Mehsana, and 27 km from Vallabhipur to Ranghola. At appraisal the social impact assessments expected impacts on about 730 project-affected households, title holders and non-title holders together, 23 hectares of private land, 7 hectares of government land and 304 privately owned structures, mostly shops, from the widening and strengthening works. Three of the corridors passed through Schedule V areas with tribal populations, and the appraisal document recorded three Scheduled Tribe households as affected. In the event, 14.4 hectares of land were acquired during implementation, of which 11.51 hectares were private. Acquisition in the eight corridors took two years. The notification of acquisition was issued in January 2017 under local law, but the notification awarding compensation could only be issued in February 2019, two years later. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the completion report reports no issues with compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy, and that the lengthy land acquisition process delayed implementation and hurt the project's efficiency. District-level grievance redressal committees were set up to take complaints about resettlement and compensation, alongside postal correspondence and approaches to the executive engineers on site. Some religious structures affected by the works were relocated with the cooperation of local communities.
gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4,000 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The only count of people in the documents opened is the appraisal estimate of about 730 project-affected households in the Project Appraisal Document, repeated in the ICR Review. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2020 with the full US$175 million disbursed. No Implementation Completion and Results Report for this project is disclosed in the Bank's document archive; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it, dated 13 June 2022, is the latest public account found.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-48430 for the Punjab State Road Sector Project (P090585). US$250 million approved 5 December 2006; US$248,110,727.51 disbursed against a total project cost of US$407.3 million. Original closing 5 June 2012; the project was restructured at level 2 in August 2012 and again on 10 November 2014, and closed 5 June 2017, five years late. Environmental Category A, with the policies on environmental assessment, forests, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement triggered (IEG ICR Review, 8 May 2018; World Bank Project Appraisal Document, 10 November 2006).

dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.community: At Dehlon, where the project built a bypass, one of the owners of a plot refused the compensation offered in May 2017 and filed a case in the High Court; a complaint had already gone to the Bank's Grievance Redress Service in December 2016. In April 2017 the contractors tried to start work on the plot and the Bank team insisted all work stop until compensation was settled. Soon after the project closed on 5 June 2017 the contractor went back onto the plot and finished building the bypass. The plaintiff did not appear at the High Court hearing of 31 January 2018 and the hearing was rescheduled for the end of March 2018. The Bank's task team leader told the Independent Evaluation Group that half of the co-owners have been paid, that the co-owner who complained is still pursuing the matter in the High Court, and that the matter has not been resolved. There was also a built harm from the drainage works: in 2009 the project team found that drains built in urban areas sat above the plinth level of the buildings next to them, blocking numerous commercial and residential entrances. The Independent Evaluation Group attributes this to weak monitoring and to the roads board's environment and social officers not being involved in two upgrading works, which were closed out without proper clean-up, rehabilitation or compliance reports, and to inadequate handling of the environmental management plan and work-site safety on the output and performance based road contract. The Bank team later arranged an assessment and an action plan to remedy it. At appraisal the project expected 112 people from 24 households to be marginally or temporarily affected on the rehabilitation roads with none displaced, and about 31 hectares of land to be acquired. For the upgrading roads the appraisal document gives two readings of the same impact: its main text says 4,731 people from 1,233 households would be affected at least temporarily with people from 197 households expected to be displaced, while its safeguards annex, para 10.9, says 4,731 persons would be affected from 831 households of which 1,233 would be displaced from 197 households. Both are appraisal expectations, not outcomes.
dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,977 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The appraisal document's main-text figure for people affected at least temporarily on the upgrading roads is 4,731, with people from 197 households expected to be displaced; its safeguards annex gives 1,233 as the number displaced instead. No Bank document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.killed_note: Two fatal workplace accidents happened in 2016. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records them in one sentence, citing para 66 of the completion report: 'there were two fatal workplace accidents in 2016 which were not reported to the Bank'. The Bank's team learned of them only after making a specific request to the Punjab Roads and Bridges Development Board in February 2017, and then met contractors, consultants and the board about construction zone safety and traffic management. No document opened states that the accidents happened on works financed by the project, names the dead, gives the dates or locations, says which contractor's works they occurred on, or records any compensation to their families. They are therefore left uncounted.
dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.outcome: The loan closed on 5 June 2017. The bypass across the disputed plot was completed after closing. The Bank's task team leader told the Independent Evaluation Group that half the co-owners have been paid, that the co-owner who objected has not been, and that the case continues in the High Court, with the team still following the matter up as of the review of 8 May 2018. No later account was found.

tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.title: Culvert 16/3 Drainage Dispute at Tudella, Ja-Ela

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-41380 (CR 4138-CE), IDA-44290 (CR 4429-CE) and IDA-49060 (CR 4906-LK) for the Road Sector Assistance Project (P086411) and its two additional financings. CR 4138-CE: US$100 million approved 15 December 2005, effective 16 March 2006, US$96.40 million disbursed. CR 4429-CE, first additional financing: US$98.10 million, 16 September 2008, US$83.60 million disbursed. CR 4906-LK, second additional financing (P116742): US$100 million, which the Inspection Panel notice dates to 29 April 2011 and the Panel's project information to 12 April 2011, US$75.00 million disbursed. Original total commitment XDR 69.10 million, revised and disbursed XDR 180.16 million, with XDR 12.14 million cancelled. Original closing 30 September 2011; actual closing 30 June 2015. Category B. Outcome rated Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome High. The implementing agency was the Road Development Authority under the Ministry of Ports and Highways (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 June 2016; Inspection Panel Notice of Non-Registration, 10 November 2014).

tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.community: On 24 March 2014 the World Bank Inspection Panel received a request for inspection, dated 25 February 2014, from five named people living in Tudella, Ja-Ela, near culvert 16/3 on the A3 Colombo-Puttalam road: M. J. R. Perera, M. N. D. Perera, Shirley Dias, Anthony Suriyarachchi and B. A. R. Mallika, writing for themselves and others. Their complaint concerned the rebuilt and enlarged culvert 16/3, financed by the project's second additional financing, which drains rainwater from the A3 into a private drain on Mr Perera's land. One of the requesters told the Panel that 67 individuals were affected by the handling of rainwater near the culvert and that about eight properties were likely to be hit. They said the enlarged culvert and the new side drains connected to it would push more water into the private drain than it could hold, worsening flooding that already happened in the area, and that the culvert channels water in the opposite direction to the natural slope of the land. On 26 January 2014 they closed the private trench permanently, in response to written requests and petitions from residents who feared flooding of houses on the opposite side of the street; Bank management told the Panel that this closure was in turn increasing flooding for neighbours elsewhere. The Road Development Authority offered to lay an underground hume pipe across Mr Perera's property in place of the open drain; he refused, treating construction on his land as a threat to his legal ownership and to the property's resale value, and Bank management found his own alternative not technically feasible for lack of elevation at the site. Mr Perera petitioned the Court of Appeal of Sri Lanka (C.A. Application No. 138/2014) over whether the drain on his land is private or public. The court granted an injunction halting construction on his property, and that injunction was still in force when the Panel wrote. On 10 November 2014 the Panel declined to register the request, because the question turned on the interpretation of local law, which is outside its mandate, and because, in the Panel's words, the likelihood of harm from possible flooding potentially exacerbated by the project was not occurring at that time. Separately, the completion report records that the project received over 4,000 public complaints, all but two of which were resolved on site; more than 60 per cent concerned access to houses, 25 per cent access to roads and 10 per cent retaining and parapet walls. The report attributes the drainage problems to the designs of culverts and drains not being settled up front. It also states that no physical or economic displacement of people or resettlement impacts were experienced, and that most of the land used to widen the roads was already held by the Road Development Authority or was obtained through voluntary land donations from project beneficiaries.
tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,386 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report states that the project caused no physical or economic displacement of people at all. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.outcome: The credits closed on 30 June 2015. The Inspection Panel request was not registered, and the Panel noted that the requesters keep the right to file again on new evidence. The Court of Appeal case over whether the drain is private or public, and with it whether project-financed works may proceed on the property, was unresolved when the Panel wrote on 10 November 2014, with an injunction in force. No later account of either the court case or the drainage was found.

tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.confidence_note: The named requesters, the figures of 67 individuals and about eight properties, the court application number and the injunction are all taken from the Inspection Panel's own Notice of Non-Registration. The weakness is in what the documents say actually happened. The Panel found that the flooding harm alleged was not occurring at the time, so the central claim is of harm feared rather than suffered. The increased flooding for neighbours is attributed by Bank management to the requesters' own closure of the trench, not to the works. The Bank's completion report says there was no displacement and no resettlement impact. The 4,000-plus complaints about house and road access are counted by the completion report but not described, and all but two were resolved on site, so it is not known what loss, if any, people suffered. The land obtained through 'voluntary land donations from project beneficiaries' is recorded with no figure for how much land or how many donors.
tudella-jaela-a3-culvert-complaint.reason: Cut on test 2 (actual harm) and on the forward rule. The Inspection Panel's Notice of Non-Registration of 10 November 2014 states, under 'Panel's Determination': 'The likelihood of harm from possible flooding potentially exacerbated by the Project, as alleged in the Request, is not occurring at this time.' Every flooding impact in the request is forward-looking in the Panel's own rendering - 'may flood their properties', 'likely to be impacted is eight', 'possibly lead to displacement'. The one increase in flooding in the record is attributed by Bank management to the requesters' own closure of the private trench on 26 January 2014. Limb (a) fails on the completion report's para 47: 'no physical or economic displacement of persons or resettlement impacts were experienced by the Project'. Limb (b) fails on the only remaining content, the complaint count: that count sits in Annex 7 Part 1, the Road Development Authority's own completion report, at para 12, which reads 'RSAP received over 4000 complaints; all but two were resolved on site. More than 60 percent of the public complaints or requests were related to house access, 25 percent to road access'. It counts complaints and requests, not losses; it describes no loss to any person; and it records all but two as resolved on site. 'Over 4000' is a floor, not a count. The two unresolved complaints are not identified or described. The Court of Appeal injunction halts construction on the requester's property, which is a harm prevented rather than suffered.

salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.title: Sixty-Five Squatter Families Moved into Flats at Salem, and Land Taken in Chennai
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.place: Salem city, Tamil Nadu, with land acquisition under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, India
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.point: Salem, the one town under the project's urban investment component where resettlement took place (OpenStreetMap administrative point for Salem, Tamil Nadu)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-47980 for the Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project (P083780). US$300 million approved 5 July 2005 and effective 19 October 2005; US$290.87 million disbursed. Original closing 30 March 2011; actual closing 31 March 2014. The project was restructured twice: the completion report's text dates the restructurings to August 2009 and January 2012, while its own data sheet dates them to 1 July 2009 and 7 February 2012. It financed 110 sub-projects under the urban investment component as well as the Chennai urban transport sub-component, and paid rehabilitation and resettlement costs: under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, the completion report's cost table gives INR 137.22 million at appraisal for rehabilitation and resettlement together with shifting of utilities, against INR 191.2 million actually spent (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 September 2014; IEG ICR Review ICRR14687, 12 May 2015).

salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.community: Under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, 212 title holders and 337 non-title holders were affected, including the resettlement of five displaced families. The cost of private land acquisition and resettlement and rehabilitation assistance there was INR 132.32 million, about US$2.20 million, or 8.5 per cent of that sub-component's cost. Under the urban investment component, 110 sub-projects were carried out; private land acquisition was involved in only seven of them and resettlement in one. In all, 21 hectares of private land were acquired from 31 landowners, and about 45 hectares of government land were transferred, including 23 acres of temple land. The resettlement took place in Salem, where 65 squatter families were moved into multi-storied apartments. Total compensation and resettlement assistance for those eight sub-projects came to INR 30 million, 0.73 per cent of their cost. The completion report records instances of delays in paying compensation and resettlement assistance, later addressed after follow-up by the Bank team and the state's urban development fund. At loan closure all compensation and assistance had been paid, except that the 65 families moved into the Salem apartment had not been given title to their flats: under Tamil Nadu rules titles were to be issued in December 2014, at the end of a five-year stay. An end-term impact evaluation of the Salem families found their incomes up, because more family members were working, and their housing better, having moved from huts to built flats. The same evaluation recorded what was wrong: drinking water supply was erratic and flats on the upper floors got no water because of problems lifting it; allotment of flats took no account of the elderly, old and sick, some of whom were put on higher floors; and residents reported thefts and a lack of security. The families kept ties to where they had lived, still sending children to schools there, visiting doctors there and mostly still working there. A separate evaluation of the Chennai transport families found 75 per cent satisfied with the rate of compensation, which the report attributes to a consent award process for private land and payment for structures without depreciation; compensation money was mostly spent on improving houses, 40 per cent of it. Land availability was a running problem: about 16 of the more than 40 sites needed for urban sub-projects had to be changed, for reasons including objections from nearby residents and court cases over unclear land titles.
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.displaced_label: families relocated (65 squatter families at Salem, 5 displaced families under the Chennai urban transport sub-component)
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,300 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 65 squatter families resettled at Salem and five displaced families resettled under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, 70 families in all, alongside 212 title holders and 337 non-title holders affected in Chennai and 31 landowners whose land was acquired.
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.outcome: The loan closed on 31 March 2014 with the 65 Salem families living in the flats but without title to them, which was due in December 2014. The Bank advised Salem Corporation to act on the impact evaluation's findings and to issue the titles when due. No document found records whether the titles were issued.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-81360 for the Assam State Roads Project (P096018). US$320 million approved 13 March 2012. The completion report's financing table gives the loan's original and revised commitment as US$320,000,000 and US$280,777,402 disbursed, with the loan and the trust fund grant together committing US$321,750,000, revised to US$321,748,396, and US$282,525,798 disbursed; it puts the actual total project cost at US$282,525,798 against US$401,750,000 at appraisal. The Independent Evaluation Group's data sheet instead shows US$321,748,396.16 as the revised IBRD commitment and US$284,447,922.45 as the total project cost. Original closing 31 March 2018; restructured at level 2 on 29 March 2018 and closed 30 September 2019, 18 months late. Among the works the loan paid for was resettlement and rehabilitation assistance to project-affected people, and the Bank suspended work on one package until compensation was paid (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 March 2020; IEG ICR Review ICRR0022128, 26 June 2020).

lenders.name: World Bank, trust fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-11446 alongside the loan: US$1,750,000 committed, revised to US$1,748,396, all of it disbursed (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 March 2020).

assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.community: The project upgraded and rehabilitated roads in Assam, 978 km by closing against a revised target of 1,000 km. At appraisal, social screening covered about 420 km of roads, with a census and socio-economic survey of the people in every structure and on all land within the corridor of impact for Phase I of the upgrading component. The assessment concluded that widening to two lanes would not need extensive resettlement because the work would mostly stay inside the existing right of way, and that about 80 per cent of the land needed was already available in stretches along the Phase I corridors. On one of the project's packages that broke down. The completion report states plainly that the project departed from the agreements reached under the Resettlement Action Plan and that the land and properties were acquired without paying compensation to the owners. As a corrective measure, work on the affected package was suspended until the required processes were completed and the compensation funds were transferred. The completion report says compensation was otherwise largely paid on time, 'barring for one package'. The completion report records the remaining activity of compensation payment for land acquisition as settled, confirmed by the completion report mission. The Independent Evaluation Group repeats the episode and adds what the project team told it by email on 10 June 2020: that for the first three years no designated staff was involved in the land acquisition process, and that after the department strengthened its environment and social cell in the second half of the project 'all the compensation was fully paid, and all the land acquisition issues were amicably settled'. The project also could not obtain utilisation certificates for money spent on land acquisition and utility shifting by other state agencies, which the state met from its own funds, and the project's financial management rating was lowered to unsatisfactory for a year after it took two years to answer the Auditor General's inspection report. The policy on indigenous peoples was triggered at appraisal because some corridors were expected to pass through areas where indigenous communities had settled, and an Indigenous Peoples Development Plan was prepared, but the completion report states the policy was never applied during implementation because the project did not pass through any major tribal settlements.
assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,891 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated, and no document found says how many owners had their land and property taken without payment on the affected package.
assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.outcome: The loan closed on 30 September 2019. Work on the package where land and property had been taken without payment was suspended until the compensation was transferred, and the completion report records the outstanding land acquisition compensation as settled. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 26 June 2020 repeats that there was one package where land and properties were acquired without compensation, and reports the project team's statement that all compensation was eventually paid.

_dropped_P110051_haryana_power.reason: Haryana Power System Improvement Project (P110051): no actual harm found. The completion report of 25 June 2018 and the Independent Evaluation Group review of 21 November 2018 record that Haryana State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd acquired all the land, which the completion report describes as government land, and legally transferred it to the transmission company; that INR 1,654,749,000 was paid across 33 transmission sub-projects against crop compensation, forest compensation, railways and Haryana Urban Development Authority costs, and land cost; and that three sub-projects were dropped or moved to other sites after community agitation. No relocation, no unpaid compensation and no arrests are recorded. The completion report records 'two accidents under the project due to negligence' and does not state that anyone was killed or injured, so no death is counted. The two documents disagree on how many packages needed resettlement plans: the completion report says 'nearly 11 packages', the review says ten. ICIJ gives 3,907 for this project.

_dropped_P128966_fata_rural_roads.reason: MDTF FATA Emergency Rural Roads Project (P128966): no actual harm found. The completion report of 18 May 2016 and the Independent Evaluation Group review of 28 February 2017 record that all land procured was agricultural, that no residential land was taken and no resettlement was needed, that compensation claims were processed and paid, and that affected people expressed general satisfaction, with a few landowners saying the rates should have been higher given inflation. No count of affected people, no relocation, no unpaid compensation, no arrests and no deaths tied to the project are recorded. The project did fail to comply with the Bank's environmental safeguards, with almost no mitigation measures implemented at the sites and no environmental monitoring, but no harm to identifiable people is recorded from that. The completion report also records that two suicide attacks occurred while the project was being implemented, given as a cause of delay, not attributed to the project or its contractors and with no statement that anyone was killed; that sentence belongs to this project and not to the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa roads project. ICIJ gives 3,829 for this project.
